item.title: Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will hold ‘Christmases Not Forgotten’ for WWII survivors

item.content:encoded:
The Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will host Christmases Not Forgotten, a gathering honoring Guam’s World War II survivors who missed out on celebrating Christmas during the Japanese occupation.

The event is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Dec. 6 at the Zefiro Ballroom at LeoPalace Resort. It will bring together manåmko’ and their families for an afternoon of fellowship, music, dining, and honoring those whose lives were lost and those who survived WWII.

The Christmases Not Forgotten was created by a committee of the Mañenggon Memorial Foundation, including war survivor advisors Julia Villagomez, Rosa “Tan Chai” Duenas and David D.L. Flores. Foundation founders Willy Flores and Rita Franquez organized the gathering after hearing survivors share their experiences during and after the war. Flores said many survivors recalled missing family being together and gatherings of Christmas celebrations between 1941 and 1944.

Flores and Franquez said survivors recalled that during the war, some were able to say nobenas, or the CHamoru rosary, in secret.

“They could not get together openly, and they definitely could not celebrate Christmas,” Flores said. “They talked about how Christmas was taken from them in 1941, then of course 42, 43, and then 44. Even though the island was basically freed in July and August, still there was no time to put together Christmas in 44.”

The gathering will include live entertainment, a special surprise appearance, a visit from Santa Claus, gifts, and a shared meal. The foundation said their goal is to honor and celebrate the manåmko’ of Guam and those who have survived and lost their lives in WWII.

Admission is free for Guam WWII survivors. Individual tickets are $65. Family tables and corporate sponsorship opportunities are also available.

The foundation hopes the gathering will help preserve their stories and ensure future generations understand the experiences and sacrifices of those who lived through the war.

item.content:encoded:
CNMI Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds has requested a briefing from the U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, to discuss concerns about illicit financial activity and the potential role of Chinese money laundering networks in the Commonwealth.

In a Nov. 18 letter to FinCEN acting Director Jenna Casanova, King-Hinds said federal investigations and prosecutions over the years have highlighted concerns about money laundering and other financial crimes linked to Chinese capital in the CNMI.

The delegate said more information is needed to understand how such networks operate, whether they remain active in the Northern Marianas and what steps federal and local officials can take to address potential risks.

King-Hinds requested a briefing with FinCEN officials to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by criminal organizations and to explore possible legislative, regulatory and enforcement measures to strengthen prevention efforts.

She said the CNMI's proximity to East Asia, its integration into the U.S. financial system and its economic ties to the region warrant closer examination of financial crime risks.

King-Hinds said protecting legitimate investment and economic activity while preventing illicit financial networks from exploiting local institutions is critical to the Commonwealth's economic and security interests.

item.content:encoded:
Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero has declared the day after Thanksgiving - Black Friday - a government of Guam holiday, giving government employees an additional day off this week

In an executive order issued Monday, Leon Guerrero designated Nov. 27 as a government holiday. All executive branch departments and agencies will be closed that day, with the exception of essential personnel and operations deemed necessary by agency heads to protect public health, safety and welfare.

The governor said the additional holiday recognizes the work of public servants while allowing families more time to spend together during the holiday season.

Lt. Gov. Joshua Tenorio also encouraged residents to support local businesses over the extended holiday weekend and practice inafa’maolek by looking out for one another on the roads and in their neighborhoods.

Residents are encouraged to plan ahead for any government services they may need before the Friday closure.

item.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
item.description: Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings. "I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
item.content:encoded:
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff , a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving . "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation , an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

item.title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
item.description: Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday. This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation .
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.

This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation .

But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.

Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.

Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.

Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.

After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.

"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."

Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.

"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."

Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.

If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).

These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.

Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.

Yet Meta also has long been accused of violating user privacy, as in a 2022 case about improperly sharing user data . Meta did not admit to wrongdoing but settled for about $725 million.

Beyond Meta, there are cases of AI jumping guardrails that programmers set for it. Users have also reported their AI agents acting without their consent, such as sending their home address to a buyer from Facebook Marketplace and booking a hotel .

Philip Bruno, chief strategy and growth officer with ACI Worldwide, says he would share what he's shopping for with AI, but warns to be more careful with personal information.

"I'm cooking for a family of four. That is fine to be able to say," Bruno says. "I would be very careful about payment information."

On that note, experts caution shoppers to be careful with other people's information. It's easy to give most AIs loads of information about your father while brainstorming his gift. Know AI agents can also use this to build profiles of the shopper's friends and family . Being illusive and not specifying who you're shopping for during the brainstorming can help.

One major selling point for using AI agents is that they can check multiple websites and compare prices, bringing them for human review all in one spot. That does not mean the first price it shows you is the best one.

"One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that it somehow sees everything," Pfeiffer says. "That's just false. It gets you the best answer it can as quickly as possible."

AI agents still need time to hunt for deals. Many will often let shoppers watch along as they browse the web, rather than relying on preset knowledge.

This automating can also mean time savings for the user. Agents often can run in the background 24/7.

If users are in no particular holiday rush, they can leave the AI to continue shopping for weeks or even months, only sending a notice when a price drops into a budget friendly range.

Just know these agents don't always have access to every website. Amazon, for example, blocks Muse, arguing Meta did not alert Amazon of plans and that agents did not identify themselves while browsing.

For all the advances since ChatGPT's launch four years ago, AI still hallucinates and makes mistakes.

Visa recently released a report warning buyers to beware of AI shoppers. It tested different AI models and found they failed to recommend a product that met a customer's needs in 42% of test runs – more than half of those still recommended a product that didn't match.

That provides even more reason to click through and read up on whatever potential gift an AI recommends to make sure it's what shoppers want.

Otherwise people may find themselves turning back to that same AI agent for help making a return.

item.content:encoded:
As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.

Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.

A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.
